title: What is CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery): attacker tricks a logged-in user's browser into making an unwanted request to your server: and how to prevent it (CSRF token in forms, SameSite cookie attribute)?
shortTitle: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) and How to Prevent It
topicTitle: Web Vulnerabilities: SQLi, XSS, CSRF, SSRF
keyPoints: CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted, state-changing request to a site where the user is already authenticated.
It works because browsers automatically attach cookies to any request to a domain, regardless of which site initiated it.
The synchronizer token pattern embeds an unguessable anti-CSRF token in forms that the attacker cannot read or guess.
The SameSite cookie attribute (Strict or Lax) tells the browser not to attach cookies on cross-site requests.
Token-based APIs with Authorization headers are not CSRF-prone because browsers do not auto-attach custom headers.
Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default for session-based applications.

s1_definition.oneliner: CSRF rides the victim's auto-sent cookie; stop it with an unguessable token and SameSite cookies.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)** – an attack that tricks a victim's browser into sending an unwanted, state-changing request to a site where the victim is already authenticated.
- **Root cause** – the browser automatically attaches cookies to any request to a domain, regardless of which site initiated it.
- **Synchronizer token** – a secret, per-session anti-CSRF token embedded in forms or headers that the attacker cannot read or guess.
- **SameSite attribute** – a cookie attribute (`Strict` or `Lax`) that stops the browser from sending the cookie on cross-site requests.
- **Not affected** – APIs that use `Authorization: Bearer` headers instead of cookies, because browsers do not auto-attach custom headers.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh is logged into National Bank of India in one tab. In another tab he visits a malicious site that secretly contains a hidden form which auto-submits a transfer request to the bank. Because the browser automatically attaches Rajesh's bank cookie, the bank sees a seemingly valid transfer instruction and obeys it. A CSRF token is like the bank requiring a secret one-time stamp that only its own genuine pages print; the malicious site cannot know the stamp, so its forged instruction is rejected.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  CSRF Attack:
  ┌──────────┐  visits evil.com   ┌──────────┐
  │  Rajesh  ├───────────────────►│ evil.com │
  │ (logged  │                    │          │
  │  into    │◄───────────────────┤ Hidden   │
  │  bank)   │  auto-submits form │ form     │
  └──────┬───┘  to bank.com       └──────────┘
         │
         │  POST /transfer (cookie auto-attached)
         ▼
  ┌──────────────┐
  │  Bank Server │
  │  Sees valid  │
  │  cookie!     │── No CSRF token ──► REJECT (if protected)
  │              │── Valid CSRF token ──► ALLOW (legitimate)
  └──────────────┘
```

```text
  Defense Layers:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Layer 1: SameSite=Strict             │
  │   Browser refuses to send cookie     │
  │   on cross-site requests             │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Layer 2: CSRF Token                  │
  │   Server rejects requests without    │
  │   the correct unguessable token      │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Layer 3: Origin/Referer Check        │
  │   Server verifies request origin     │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Layer 4: Idempotent GETs             │
  │   No state changes on GET requests   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Cross-Site Request Forgery, or CSRF, is an attack that tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted, state-changing request to a site where the user is already authenticated. It works because browsers automatically attach cookies to any request to a domain, so a forged request from a malicious page carries the victim's valid session cookie and the server believes it is genuine. The attacker never needs to read the response; the harm is the side effect, like a transfer or a changed email.

In the National Bank of India project, the scenario is Rajesh logged into the bank in one tab while a malicious page in another tab auto-submits a transfer to the attacker. Because the browser attaches his session cookie, the bank would almost execute it. The defense relied on first is the synchronizer token pattern: the bank embeds an unguessable anti-CSRF token in its own pages and requires it on every state-changing request. The attacker's cross-site page cannot read that token because the same-origin policy blocks it, so the forged request is rejected.

The second defense is the SameSite cookie attribute set to Strict or Lax, which tells the browser not to attach the session cookie on cross-site requests at all, neutralizing most CSRF at the browser level. A legitimate transfer with the correct token succeeds, a forged transfer without the token is rejected, and SameSite=Strict refuses to send the cookie cross-site. Both are combined for defense in depth.

The nuance that separates a senior answer is that CSRF specifically affects cookie-based authentication. APIs that send credentials in the Authorization header with a bearer token are not CSRF-prone, because the browser does not automatically attach custom headers.

Remember one sentence: CSRF rides the auto-sent cookie, so block it with an unguessable token the attacker cannot read and SameSite cookies the browser will not send cross-site.
